summary: Gives guidelines for applying or extending MPLS and GMPLS protocols and clarifies the IETF working groups' responsibility for them. It targets multi-vendor forums and other standards bodies, and stresses using IETF review procedures. It is a best current practice.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4929 sets out the only accepted way to propose a change to the MPLS and GMPLS protocols: write down what is needed, have the IETF working group that owns those protocols check the requirements, and then develop and review the solution in the same open process. A forum that skips those steps will not get the IETF's endorsement or any IANA code points.

subtitle: How a change to the MPLS and GMPLS protocols has to travel before it can become a standard.

tldr.problem: Standards bodies outside the IETF wanted to extend the MPLS protocol suites, and doing it outside the IETF produced conflicting extensions that made the protocols harder to implement and interoperate.
tldr.mechanism: The document defines one route: a requirements statement Internet-Draft is evaluated by the working group that owns the protocols, and the solution is written and reviewed in the same process, with explicit rules for rejecting work and for refusing to endorse it.
tldr.outcome: RFC 4929 is BCP 129 and is not obsoleted. It does not change the IETF's own process; it applies the existing process to MPLS and GMPLS.

facts.label: Protocol owners
facts.value: MPLS working group and CCAMP working group

today: RFC 4929 is a Best Current Practice document, BCP 129, and is neither obsoleted nor updated by any RFC listed for it. It does not change the IETF standards process; it applies the process described in RFC 4775 to the MPLS and GMPLS protocols.

sections.title: Why a Change Process for MPLS and GMPLS
sections.content:
The MPLS and GMPLS technology is developed in two main tracks in the IETF. MPLS refers to the work done for packet switched networks, while GMPLS refers to the efforts to apply the MPLS protocols to all types of networks including packet and non-packet technologies. Though GMPLS is by definition a superset of MPLS, the term (G)MPLS is used in this document to indicate both tracks.

RFC 4775 discusses procedural issues related to the extension or variation of IETF protocols by other standards development organizations, and recommends that major extensions to, or variations of, IETF protocols only take place through normal IETF processes or in coordination with the IETF.

The (G)MPLS protocol families were developed within the IETF and constitute significant protocol suites within the Internet standards, and they have become popular for a number of new applications and deployment scenarios. There have been concerns about other technology fora developing, using and publishing non-standard protocol extensions as a standard, not only for use within their community but for wider industry use. Especially concerning is the development of extensions without consulting the (G)MPLS working groups, which are then presented to the working group as a fait accompli.

Defining and publishing non-standard extensions by other fora, without IETF review and outside the IETF publication process, whether rationalized as limited to use among forum vendors, limited to a particular application, or allowing timely demonstrations, has the unfortunate potential to hinder interoperability and increase the complexity of the protocol, sow confusion in the industry, and circumvent the standards process that exists to ensure protocol implementability. Non-standard extensions, including experimental values, are not to be portrayed as industrial standards whether by an individual vendor, an industry forum or a standards body.

The document clarifies the roles of the IETF's MPLS and Common Control and Measurement Plane (CCAMP) working groups and documents the required use of the RFC 4775 procedure for fora wishing to apply or extend the (G)MPLS protocols. The IETF cannot enforce a forum to use the (G)MPLS change procedure, though any forum not following it, when applying for IANA assignment or IETF publication, will be delayed until the procedure has been completed. The document does not change the formal IETF standards process, and is consistent with the general procedures for protocol extensions defined in RFC 4775.
sections.plainLanguage: The problem is not technical but procedural. When a trade body publishes its own extension of a protocol, vendors end up with incompatible versions and the protocol becomes harder to implement. This document says that any change to these protocols has to go through the ordinary IETF route, and explains what that route is.

sections.title: Who Owns the (G)MPLS Protocols in the IETF
sections.content:
Two working groups in the IETF's Routing Area are responsible for work related to developing the (G)MPLS technologies: the Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS) working group and the Common Control and Measurement Plane (CCAMP) working group.

The MPLS working group is responsible for standardizing the base technology that uses label switching, and for describing the implementation of Label Switched Paths (LSPs) over various packet and frame-based link level technologies. Its charter includes procedures and protocols for the distribution of labels between routers, as well as encapsulations, operation and management, traffic engineering and multicast considerations. The document assumes that the MPLS working group remains the chartered authority on MPLS technologies, but notes that the IETF may appoint another working group to handle specific extensions or changes, and that if the MPLS working group completes its work and is closed, the IETF will use the non-working group standards track document process with designated experts from the community.

The CCAMP working group coordinates the work within the IETF defining common control and measurement planes for ISP and SP core tunneling technologies. This includes defining signalling and measurement protocols so that they support multiple physical path and tunnel technologies using input from technology-specific working groups such as the MPLS working group, and it includes the development of protocol-independent metrics and parameters for describing links and paths. The technology that the CCAMP working group focuses on is called Generalized MPLS, indicating that CCAMP addresses a generalized technology where labels are defined so that they are compatible with the technology over which the data is transported. While the MPLS working group focuses on packet- and frame-switched technologies, CCAMP focuses on common methods across a broad spectrum of switching technologies, so GMPLS can be viewed as a superset of MPLS.

The two groups sometimes divide work differently from their charters, as with point-to-multipoint traffic engineering LSPs. An entity or individual wishing to propose extensions or changes to (G)MPLS should first decide which of the two working groups will take the proposal, though the chairs, in conjunction with their Area Directors, may redirect it.

Other working groups also relate to (G)MPLS. The IP over Optical working group and the Internet Traffic Engineering working group focus on problem statements and requirements and have not specified any protocols. The Bidirectional Forwarding Detection working group is chartered for requirements evaluation and protocol specification for BFD. The Layer 2 VPN and Layer 3 VPN working groups have been chartered to specify a limited number of solutions for provider provisioned VPNs, and much of their work does not include specifying new protocols. The Layer 1 VPN working group is chartered to specify the mechanisms necessary for providing Layer 1 VPN services over a GMPLS-enabled transport network, and will not develop GMPLS protocol extensions in isolation but will develop requirements and propose extensions that will be reviewed and approved by the (G)MPLS working groups. The Pseudo Wire Emulation End to End working group may use the (G)MPLS protocols in its specifications. The procedures in this document apply to all organizations outside the IETF whether or not they have formal liaison relationships with the IETF.
sections.plainLanguage: Two groups are in charge: the MPLS group for label switching in packet and frame networks, and the CCAMP group for the general case of many kinds of transport technology, which is where GMPLS comes from. Other groups may use these protocols, but they ask the owning groups for changes rather than making them.

sections.title: The Change Process in Outline
sections.content:
Whenever there is reason to believe that a particular problem may be solved by use of or extensions to the (G)MPLS protocols, a communication using the formal liaison process, or an informal communication for a forum without a formal relationship, may be used to discuss the problem with the IETF. Collaboration with the IETF in the early discussion phase facilitates a timely understanding of whether the problem has already been solved, may be outside the scope of the (G)MPLS protocols, or may require more investigation.

Whenever any extension or change is desired, a problem statement and/or requirements statement must be produced and submitted to the IETF as an Internet-Draft. When the requirements come from an external organization, informal communications such as e-mail to working group mailing lists is strongly encouraged, and the Internet-Draft may instead be submitted through a formal liaison statement. Formal communication reduces the risk of confusing an individual participant's opinion for that of the group, though it introduces a more lengthy communication cycle.

The IETF, through the appropriate Area Director and the chairs of the MPLS and CCAMP working groups, will direct the requirements draft to an appropriate working group for assessment and comment. In assessing the requirements statement, the IETF may determine that the requirements can be satisfied without modifications to the protocols; that they are not sufficiently general, or that there is not sufficient interest to warrant a standards-track change; that they justify a standards-track change; that they might not be possible to satisfy without violating the (G)MPLS architecture in a way that would harm the technology; or that they should be combined with other requirements to solve a more general problem or the same problem in a more flexible way.

In the event that the IETF agrees to develop a solution, it will set milestones that result in timely delivery. If the IETF rejects the requirements, this will only be done with clear explanation and full discussion with the source of the requirements.

Solutions developed within the IETF may be sourced from external organizations and presented for review, discussion, modification and adoption as Internet-Drafts, and may be presented in advance of the completion of the requirements work. All solutions will be processed through the normal IETF process with other proposed solutions. A solution draft is adopted as an IETF working group draft when the requirements are stable, and not before the protocol-responsible working group has a charter item to cover the solutions work. It is not recommended for the source forum to continue working on solutions in parallel with work in the IETF.
sections.plainLanguage: Talk to the IETF early, write down what you need, and let the owning working group judge it. The judgement can be that existing protocols already do the job, that the request is too narrow to be worth a standard, that it is worth one, or that it would break the architecture. Only the third case leads to new protocol work.

sections.title: The Stages of the Change Process
sections.content:
The preliminary investigation step is optional and is intended to provide a lightweight way to feel out the IETF's position on a proposal without writing an Internet-Draft. Its intention is to determine whether the problem has been examined already, whether the problem is in scope for the IETF, and whether solutions are already known. It is carried out informally on the mailing list of the requirements evaluation working group or on the Routing Area discussion mailing list, and may be initiated by any individual, group, external organization or IETF working group. The requirements statement evaluation phase, which allows wider IETF community participation in developing a complete requirement set, must form part of the process if the IETF is to develop protocol solutions: the process cannot move directly from the preliminary investigation phase to the development of solutions unless the working group agrees.

Before the IETF can formally pronounce on requests to change or extend the protocols, a requirements statement Internet-Draft must be written. It must be introduced by the authors to the IETF through an e-mail to the requirements evaluation working group mailing list, to the Routing Area discussion mailing list, or by a formal liaison. After discussion, the responsible Area Director must decide whether the requirements will be formally evaluated and must deliver a response that is sufficiently explanatory. The possible responses are illustrated as: requirements not understood and further discussion required; requirements understood but judged out of scope, in which case the originator can work on requirements and solutions and will not be impeded by the IETF; requirements understood but no protocol extensions needed, in which case it may be desirable to cooperate with an IETF working group in producing an Applicability Statement; and requirements understood with the IETF willing to develop protocol extensions.

In many cases the problem falls within the scope of an existing charter, in which case the responsible Area Directors designate the working group as the requirements evaluation working group and pass the document to it. If the problem is not covered by an existing charter, other alternatives may be used, for example rechartering, a Birds of a Feather session, or chartering a new working group. The objective of the evaluation is to determine a clear and complete statement of the requirements, which may include generating revisions in cooperation with the original authors. The originators must make themselves available to discuss the work; if they do not, the chairs may determine that there is insufficient support and may reject the requirements. The output is either a completed requirements statement accepted by working group consensus and passed through working group last call, or a rejection.

The Area Directors then review the completed requirements statement and pass it to the IESG, which reviews it and decides on its progression, and reviews any proposed charter changes for the solutions working group, which might include forming a new working group. The appropriate solutions working group then starts work on solutions following the normal IETF process. Solutions Internet-Drafts may be prepared externally or within the IETF, and may be submitted at earlier stages to assist the requirements work, but no Internet-Draft is formally considered as a solutions draft until the solutions working group has a charter item covering the work and the requirements are stable. The PSWG must consider an externally produced solutions draft for review and revision as a possible solutions draft, using the same open procedures as for any individual submission.
sections.plainLanguage: The route has named steps. An optional early chat, then a written requirements document, then the owning working group evaluates it, then the Area Directors and the IESG sign off, then a solutions working group writes and reviews the actual change. At each point somebody decides, and the decision has to be explained.

sections.title: Rejecting a Requirements Statement
sections.content:
Rejection of the requirements is a sensitive matter for the authors and must be handled with full disclosure and explanation by the IETF. All working group actions are taken in a public forum. The requirements can be rejected at various stages, and whoever makes the rejection is responsible for generating an explanation of it.

The reasons are set out in full. Requirements not understood: it was not clear what the requirements are or what problem is being addressed, and the process is expected to continue with further iterations. Out of scope for the IETF: the IETF must not constrain the authors from working on a solution, and if any (G)MPLS changes are later identified the requester must reinitiate the change procedure. No protocol extensions or changes are needed: the requirements evaluation working group must explain how the existing protocols can be used to meet them, and may cooperate with the authors in producing an Applicability Statement or a Profiles Internet-Draft.

Insufficient support within the IETF: the IETF must not restrict the authors from working on a solution, and the solution, and any requested IANA code points, shall be presented to the (G)MPLS solutions working group for review and possible publication as an Informational or Experimental RFC. Pending IETF review results, the IETF shall not block applications to IANA for code points, though the IANA requirements prescribed in the relevant RFCs must still be satisfied. Insufficient support for the work from the original requesters: if the authors do not make themselves available for discussion or do not contribute to completing the requirements statement, the IETF must not grant permission for the work to be carried out in any other organization, must not endorse the publication of any changes or extensions, and must not instruct IANA to allocate code points. Satisfying the requirements would break the technology: a recommendation will be made that some other technology be used, and again the IETF must not grant permission for the work elsewhere, endorse its publication, or instruct IANA to allocate code points.

On rejection the IETF must make a clear statement of why and what next steps are acceptable, and the communication method depends on how the original submission was made: an e-mail response copied to a mailing list so that it is archived, or a formal liaison response. Any IETF working group involved in the review or production of the drafts must be notified of the rejection and the reasons. A rejection may be appealed if it is disputed and cannot be reversed by direct discussion, using the conflict resolution and appeal mechanism of RFC 2026.
sections.plainLanguage: There are six named reasons for saying no, and each one says what happens to the request afterwards. Two of them, being out of scope and being unsupported, still leave the door open for the originator to build it outside the IETF. The others close it, and the document says so plainly.

sections.title: Abandoning the Solutions Work
sections.content:
Once the solutions work has been started by the solutions working group, it may be abandoned before completion. This can happen if the chairs determine that there is no longer working group support for doing the work, which could arise if no one, including the originators of the requirements statement, is willing to contribute to the development of a solutions Internet-Draft.

In the event that the solutions work is abandoned, the Area Directors responsible for the solutions working group must be consulted, and the originators of the requirements statement must be informed that the work has been abandoned, using a mechanism dependent on how the requirements were introduced. If the solution is abandoned in this way, work on solutions for the requirements must not be started in another forum. The status of extensions and changes to the (G)MPLS protocols with regard to the specific requirements returns to how it was before the process started, and any new examination of the requirements must commence at the top of the process. The abandonment of a solutions Internet-Draft may be appealed if it is disputed and cannot be reversed by direct discussion between the parties.
sections.plainLanguage: Work can also stop halfway, if nobody will work on it. When that happens the originators are told, the request goes back to the start, and the solution must not be picked up elsewhere.

sections.title: Protecting the Integrity of the Protocols
sections.content:
The (G)MPLS working groups are required to protect the architectural integrity of the protocols and must not extend the GMPLS architecture with features that do not have general use beyond the specific case. They also must not modify the architecture just to make some function more efficient at the expense of simplicity or generality.

The architectural implications of additions or changes must consider interoperability with existing and future versions of the protocols. The effects of adding features that overlap, or that deal with a point solution and are not general, are much harder to control with rules and risk impacting the protocol as a whole. To minimize operational and technical risks, IETF processes shall be followed for any requests on extensions to (G)MPLS protocols. The (G)MPLS solutions working group is the chartered owner of the (G)MPLS protocol, as long as the working group exists, and all changes or extensions must first be reviewed by it.
sections.plainLanguage: The owning group has a duty to keep the protocols general and simple, and to refuse one-off features that only serve a single case. It is also the group that has to see every proposed change before anything else happens to it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
All requirements statement Internet-Drafts must give full consideration to the security impact of the proposed additional features or functions, and all solutions Internet-Drafts must consider the impact on the security of the protocol extensions and on the pre-existing protocol. The document does not itself introduce any security issues for any (G)MPLS protocols.

The IETF process is itself at risk from denial of service attacks, and this document utilizes that process and adds clarity to it, so it might put the process at risk. Provided that the number of requirements statement Internet-Drafts is not unreasonable, there will be no significant impact on the process. The rate of arrival of requirements statement Internet-Drafts may be used by the IESG to detect denial of service attacks, and the IESG should act on such an event depending on the source of the document and the perceived relevance of the work, for example by discussing the issue with the management of external organizations.
sections.plainLanguage: Every proposal has to think about security, both for what it adds and for what is already there. The document also admits that the process itself can be flooded with paperwork, which is why the IESG watches the arrival rate of these drafts.
